t: Maximum Number of Ways to Partition an Array: Sliding Prefix Targets Under One Change
o:
**Understanding the problem**

A pivot p (1 <= p < n) partitions nums into two equal-sum sides; you may additionally overwrite one element with k and want the best achievable pivot count. In Example 1 ([2,-1,2], k = 3) nothing balances initially (prefix sums 2 and 1 versus total 3); setting nums[0] to 3 fixes pivot 2, so the answer is 1. Example 2's all-zero array already balances at both pivots, and no single change beats 2. Writing S for the total and P for the prefix sum before pivot p, balance is exactly 2*P == S. Changing nums[i] to k introduces D = k - nums[i]: pivots strictly right of i have their left side grow by D (need 2*P == S - D), while pivots at or left of i have their right side shrink by D (need 2*P == S + D). With n up to 10^5, rescoring all pivots for every candidate replacement costs around 10^10 operations, demanding an O(n) reformulation.
k: Everything hangs on one identity: pivot p balances iff twice its prefix sum equals the total — counting pivots becomes counting prefix values hitting a target.
Replacing nums[i] by k shifts the target by D = k - nums[i], asymmetrically: pivots right of i pursue S - D, pivots at or left of i pursue S + D.
Sweeping i left to right while transferring pivot i from a right multiset to a left multiset answers each replacement with two O(1) hash lookups.

a.n: Approach 1: Recount After Every Candidate Change
a.i: Score the untouched array, then try overwriting each index with k, recounting valid pivots from scratch via prefix sums. This mirrors the statement directly and serves as a perfect brute validator: O(n) per attempt, O(n^2) overall — correct but hopeless at n = 10^5.
s: Implement count(arr): sweep pivot positions, adding one whenever twice the running prefix equals arr's total.
Start the answer at count(nums) — the leave-unchanged option.
For each index i, temporarily assign nums[i] = k, update the answer with count(nums), then restore the old value.
a.t: O(n^2) — up to n+1 full prefix-sum scans of length n.
a.sp: O(1) extra — counters only; the array is edited in place and restored.

a.n: Approach 2: Hash-Map Sweep of Pivot Targets
a.i: Precompute all pivots keyed by their doubled prefix sum in a map called right. Sweeping the replacement index i left to right, move pivot i into a second map left as soon as it stops lying strictly right of i. With D = k - nums[i] fixed per step, the achievable pivots number right[S - D] + left[S + D] — two lookups — and the unchanged baseline is right[S]. Every candidate change is thus evaluated in constant time after linear preprocessing.
s: Compute S and insert 2*prefix[p] for every pivot p in [1, n-1] into map right.
Initialize the answer with the unchanged-array count right.get(2*S).
For each i from 0 to n-1, with D = k - nums[i]: update the answer with right[S - D] + left[S + D].
Then, if i + 1 <= n - 1, extend pref by nums[i] and transfer one occurrence of 2*pref from right to left (pivot i+1 no longer lies strictly right of future indices).
a.t: O(n) — one pass builds the maps and one sweep answers every replacement with two hash lookups.
a.sp: O(n) — up to n-1 doubled-prefix keys per map.

w:
**Takeaway**

Anchor everything on 2*prefix[p] == total; a single edit then merely slides the target by D depending on which side of the pivot it lands. Pitfalls: sign errors between S - D and S + D, forgetting the leave-unchanged baseline, and doubled prefixes overflowing 32-bit arithmetic (use 64-bit). Extensions worth mentioning: changing to any value means repeating the sweep per candidate value, and multiple changes push toward segment-tree bookkeeping.
